lessons.title: Proximate Analysis of Feed and Ingredients
lessons.body:
Proximate analysis is the basic set of tests that tells you what your feed ingredients are made of. It measures moisture, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre, ash, and nitrogen-free extract (NFE). For a fish farmer in Africa, this is how you check if the soybean meal you bought is really 44% protein or if it's been cut with sand. You don't need a fancy lab to start. Many universities and research institutes in Africa, like the National Institute for Freshwater Fisheries Research in Nigeria or the Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute, offer these tests for a small fee. A basic proximate analysis costs around $20â$50 per sample.

To take a sample, collect about 500g from different parts of the bag. Mix well and quarter it down to 200g. Dry the sample in an oven at 105Â°C for 24 hours to measure moisture. Then grind it fine. For crude protein, use the Kjeldahl method: digest with sulfuric acid, distill, and titrate. Crude fat is measured by extracting with petroleum ether in a Soxhlet apparatus. Crude fibre uses acid and alkali digestion. Ash is what remains after burning at 550Â°C. NFE is calculated by difference: 100% minus all the others.

Interpreting results is key. A good fish feed should have 28â40% crude protein, depending on the species. Catfish fingerlings need 40â45%, while tilapia grow-out needs 28â32%. If your fish meal tests below 60% protein, it's likely mixed with bone or scales. If your maize bran has more than 10% ash, it may contain sand. Keep a record of every batch. In Africa, where ingredient quality varies, regular proximate analysis saves money by catching adulteration early. It also helps you adjust your formulation to meet the nutritional needs of your fish.

lessons.title: In Vitro Digestibility Techniques
lessons.body:
In vitro digestibility means testing how well a feed is broken down in a test tube or container that mimics the fish's digestive system. It's faster and cheaper than feeding trials, and you can do it without live fish. The most common method uses enzymes like pepsin and pancreatin. You first grind your feed sample and mix it with a buffer solution at the same pH as the fish's stomach. Then you add enzymes and incubate at the fish's body temperature (around 25â30Â°C for tropical fish) for a few hours. After that, you separate the undigested part and measure how much protein or dry matter disappeared.

A simple protocol: Take 0.5g of feed, add 20ml of pepsin solution (0.2% in 0.1N HCl), and incubate at 30Â°C for 2 hours. Then neutralize and add pancreatin (0.5% in phosphate buffer, pH 7.5) and incubate for another 4 hours. Stop the reaction with trichloroacetic acid, centrifuge, and measure nitrogen in the pellet. The difference between the original nitrogen and the pellet nitrogen gives you digestibility. You can do this with basic lab equipment: a centrifuge, a pH meter, an incubator, and a Kjeldahl setup for nitrogen. Many African university labs have these.

In vitro results are not perfect, but they correlate well with in vivo trials. For example, if a feed has 85% in vitro protein digestibility, you can expect around 80â85% in vivo. This helps you quickly screen ingredients. If you're comparing local protein sources like soybean meal, groundnut cake, and fish meal, in vitro tests can tell you which one is more digestible. For a small-scale fish farmer, you can send samples to a lab. The cost is usually $10â$30 per sample. Use this method to choose the best ingredients before you invest in a full feeding trial.

lessons.title: In Vivo Digestibility Trials
lessons.body:
In vivo digestibility trials involve feeding fish and collecting their faeces to see how much of the feed they actually digest. This is the gold standard because it measures real digestion in a live animal. You need a set of tanks or hapas (net cages) and fish of uniform size. The most common method uses an inert marker like chromic oxide (0.5â1% of the diet). You mix the marker into the feed, feed the fish for a week, then collect faeces. The marker passes through undigested, so the ratio of nutrient to marker in feed and faeces tells you digestibility.

A simple setup: Use 3â5 tanks per diet, with 10â15 fish each. Acclimatize the fish for 3 days on the test diet. Then feed twice daily to apparent satiation for 7 days. Collect faeces daily by siphoning from the tank bottom, or use a faecal collection system. For tilapia, collect faeces within 30 minutes of feeding to avoid leaching. Dry the faeces and analyse for protein, fat, and marker. Calculate apparent digestibility coefficient (ADC) as: ADC = 100 â [100 Ã (marker in feed / marker in faeces) Ã (nutrient in faeces / nutrient in feed)].

In Africa, many farmers use simple hapa systems in ponds. You can make hapas from mosquito netting. Keep water quality stable: temperature 26â30Â°C, dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L, and pH 6.5â8.5. If you can't afford chromic oxide, you can use acid-insoluble ash as a natural marker. The trial takes about 2 weeks. Results help you formulate feeds that waste less and grow fish faster. For example, if your soybean meal has 90% protein digestibility but your cottonseed meal only 70%, you know to limit cottonseed. This saves money and reduces water pollution.

lessons.title: Growth Performance and Feed Conversion Ratio
lessons.body:
Growth performance and feed conversion ratio (FCR) are the most practical measures of how well your feed works. FCR is the amount of feed fed divided by the weight gain of the fish. If you feed 1.5 kg of feed and your fish gain 1 kg, FCR is 1.5. A lower FCR means better feed efficiency. For catfish, a good FCR is 1.0â1.5; for tilapia, 1.2â1.8. If your FCR is above 2.0, you are wasting money on feed.

To measure growth, start with a known number of fish and weigh them at the beginning. Then feed a measured amount daily for 4â8 weeks. Every week, sample 10% of the fish and weigh them to track growth. At the end, calculate weight gain, specific growth rate (SGR), and FCR. SGR = 100 Ã (ln final weight â ln initial weight) / days. For example, if fish grow from 10g to 50g in 30 days, SGR = 100 Ã (ln50 â ln10)/30 = 5.3% per day. Also record survival rate: number of fish at end divided by number at start, times 100.

In Africa, many farmers use local materials. You can use a simple kitchen scale for small fish and a hanging scale for larger ones. Keep records in a notebook. Compare your FCR with other farmers or extension agents. If your FCR is poor, check feed quality, feeding rate, and water quality. Overfeeding is common and wastes money. Underfeeding slows growth. A good feeding trial should have at least three replicate tanks per treatment. For small-scale farmers, you can do a simple trial with two ponds: one with your new feed, one with your old feed. Measure feed used and fish weight. This gives you real data to decide which feed is better. Good FCR means more profit.

lessons.title: Biological Evaluation of Protein Quality
lessons.body:
Protein quality is not just about how much protein is in the feed, but how well the fish can use it. Biological evaluation measures this using live fish. The most common methods are Protein Efficiency Ratio (PER), Net Protein Utilization (NPU), and Biological Value (BV). PER is weight gain divided by protein intake. If a fish gains 50g while eating 100g of protein, PER is 0.5. For good fish feed, PER should be above 1.5 for tilapia and above 2.0 for catfish. NPU is the percentage of absorbed protein that is retained. BV is the percentage of digested protein that is retained.

To run a PER trial, you need isonitrogenous diets (same protein level) and isocaloric (same energy). Feed fish for 4â6 weeks. Record feed intake and weight gain. Then calculate PER. For NPU and BV, you also need to analyse the fish carcass for nitrogen at the start and end. This requires a lab for Kjeldahl analysis. In Africa, you can collaborate with a university. The cost for carcass analysis is about $15â$25 per sample.

A practical example: You want to compare fish meal and soybean meal as protein sources for tilapia. You make two diets with 30% crude protein, one from fish meal, one from soybean meal. Feed each to three tanks of tilapia for 6 weeks. Calculate PER. If fish meal gives PER 2.0 and soybean meal gives 1.6, fish meal is better quality, but soybean is cheaper. You might use a mix. Also, consider essential amino acids. Fish meal is high in lysine and methionine; soybean is low in methionine. You can add synthetic methionine. In Africa, where fish meal is expensive, using plant proteins with amino acid supplements can reduce cost. Biological evaluation helps you find the best combination for growth and profit.

lessons.title: Designing and Conducting Feeding Trials
lessons.body:
A feeding trial is a controlled experiment to test how a feed affects fish growth, health, and feed efficiency. To design one, start with a clear objective: e.g., 'Compare growth of catfish fed Diet A (local ingredients) vs Diet B (commercial feed).' Then choose your fish: use the same species, size, and health status. A good trial has at least three replicates per treatment. For a small farm, you can use 6 hapas in a pond: 3 for Diet A, 3 for Diet B. Randomly assign fish to hapas. Each hapa should have the same number of fish (e.g., 20 fish per hapa) and similar water conditions.

Prepare the diets. Make sure they are isonitrogenous and isocaloric if you are testing protein sources. Mix ingredients thoroughly, add water, and pelletize using a simple meat mincer or hand pelletizer. Dry the pellets in the shade. Store in airtight bags. Feed the fish twice daily at 3â5% of body weight, adjusting weekly based on sampling. Keep records of feed given and fish weight. Monitor water quality: temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, and ammonia. In Africa, many trials fail because of poor water quality. Change water regularly or use aeration.

At the end of 6â8 weeks, harvest all fish and measure final weight, survival, and FCR. Analyse data using simple statistics: calculate means and standard deviations. You can use free software like Excel or R. If you have three replicates, you can do a t-test or ANOVA. For example, if Diet A gives average weight 80g and Diet B gives 65g, and the difference is statistically significant, you have evidence. Write a simple report: objective, methods, results, conclusion. Share with other farmers. Conducting a trial costs money, but it pays off by identifying the best feed. Start small, keep it simple, and be consistent.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed Evaluation and Feeding Trials for African Fish Farmers

In African fish farming, feed represents 60â70% of total production cost. Every naira, shilling, cedi or rand spent on feed must convert into fish flesh. This practical reference gives you the working tools to evaluate feed ingredients, run digestibility checks, design feeding trials, and interpret the numbers that decide whether your farm makes money or loses it. It is written for farm managers, feed millers, extension officers and agripreneurs who need results, not academic theory.

Whether you are formulating feed for Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), African catfish (Clarias gariepinus), or a mixed pond system, the same evaluation logic applies: know what is in your ingredient, know how much the fish can actually use, and measure whether the fish grows efficiently enough to pay for the feed.

Why Feed Evaluation Is a Business Decision

Cheap ingredients are not always cheap feed. A locally sourced ingredient may cost less per kilogram but deliver poor digestibility, anti-nutritional factors, or inconsistent nutrient density. The only way to know is to evaluate it. Proximate analysis tells you what nutrients are present. Digestibility techniques tell you how much the fish can absorb. Feeding trials tell you what happens to growth, survival and feed conversion at farm scale. Each layer reduces risk before you commit money to a full production run.

In regions where commercial feed prices have risen sharply and imported ingredients are subject to currency and logistics shocks, on-farm or local-mill evaluation is a competitive advantage. A farmer who can test a batch of local soybean meal, cassava peel, brewers' waste or fish processing by-product before buying in bulk protects cash flow and maintains fish performance.

Lesson 1: Proximate Analysis of Feed and Ingredients

Proximate analysis is the standard set of laboratory tests that quantify moisture, crude protein (CP), crude fat (ether extract, EE), crude fibre (CF), ash and nitrogen-free extract (NFE). It follows methods such as AOAC International protocols and is the first screening tool for any ingredient or finished feed.

For African feed formulators, the critical values are CP and EE for energy and growth, CF for digestibility penalties (especially in plant by-products), and ash as an indicator of mineral content or contamination (e.g., sand or bone). Moisture above 12% invites mould and aflatoxin risk, a serious issue in humid tropical storage.

Practical business use: before buying a truckload of any ingredient, request or commission a proximate analysis. Compare the result against your formulation assumption. If CP is 5 percentage points lower than expected, your feed is under-formulated and fish growth will suffer; you have grounds to reject or renegotiate the price.

Lesson 2: In Vitro Digestibility Techniques

In vitro digestibility simulates digestion in the laboratory using enzymes or acid/alkali hydrolysis. It is faster, cheaper and requires less fish than in vivo trials, making it ideal for screening many ingredients or comparing suppliers. Common methods include pepsin digestibility (for protein) and multi-enzyme assays that mimic gastric and intestinal conditions.

In Africa, where laboratory access and fish holding facilities may be limited, in vitro screening is a practical first filter. If an ingredient shows poor in vitro protein digestibility, it is unlikely to perform well in vivo unless processed (e.g., fermentation, extrusion, enzyme supplementation). Use it to rank ingredients and reject poor batches before committing to expensive tank or pond trials.

Limitation: in vitro results are indicative, not definitive. Anti-nutritional factors, feed processing, fish species and water temperature all modulate real digestibility. Always confirm promising candidates with an in vivo trial.

Lesson 3: In Vivo Digestibility Trials

In vivo digestibility measures the proportion of a nutrient absorbed by the live fish. The standard approach uses an inert marker such as chromic oxide (CrâOâ) or acid-insoluble ash (AIA) in the feed, then analyses marker and nutrient concentrations in faeces. Apparent digestibility coefficient (ADC) is calculated as:

ADC (%) = 100 Ã [1 â (marker in feed / marker in faeces) Ã (nutrient in faeces / nutrient in feed)]

For African catfish and tilapia, faecal collection systems include settling columns, siphoning, or stripping. The choice affects accuracy. Stripping is common in catfish research in Nigeria and Ghana but can underestimate digestibility if faeces are not fully evacuated.

Business value: a feed with high protein but low ADC wastes money. If 30% of the protein passes through undigested, you are paying for nutrients that end up in pond sediment, driving water quality problems and higher aeration costs.

Lesson 4: Growth Performance and Feed Conversion Ratio

Growth trials measure weight gain, specific growth rate (SGR), survival, and feed conversion ratio (FCR). FCR is the kilogrammes of feed required to produce one kilogramme of fish biomass:

FCR = Feed offered (kg, dry basis) / Fish biomass gain (kg, wet basis)

Lower FCR means better efficiency. In African tilapia and catfish production, FCRs typically range from 1.2 to 2.0 depending on feed quality, species, size, water quality and management. An FCR above 2.0 usually signals overfeeding, poor feed quality, or health stress.

Table 1: Typical growth and FCR benchmarks for Nile tilapia and African catfish in African pond/tank systems
Species Initial weight (g) Final weight (g) SGR (%/day) FCR Survival (%)
Nile tilapia 20 250 1.8â2.5 1.4â1.8 85â95
African catfish 10 500 2.5â3.5 1.0â1.5 80â92
Nile tilapia (cage) 50 400 1.5â2.2 1.5â1.9 90â98

Sources: Hecht (2007), Regional Review on Aquaculture Development: Sub-Saharan Africa, FAO Fisheries Circular No. 1017/4; FAO (2020), The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture; field benchmarks compiled from African catfish and tilapia trials reported in the African Journal of Aquatic Science and Aquaculture Reports.

Lesson 5: Biological Evaluation of Protein Quality

Not all protein is equal. Biological value (BV), protein efficiency ratio (PER), net protein utilisation (NPU) and essential amino acid index (EAAI) assess how well a protein source supports growth. For fish, the critical amino acids are lysine, methionine, threonine and tryptophan.

In African feed formulation, plant proteins such as soybean meal, groundnut cake and cottonseed meal are common, but they are often deficient in methionine or lysine. Blending with fishmeal, poultry by-product meal or synthetic amino acids improves protein quality. PER is simple to calculate in a growth trial:

PER = Weight gain (g) / Protein fed (g)

Higher PER means better protein utilisation. Use this alongside FCR to judge whether an ingredient or formulation delivers value per unit of protein purchased.

Table 2: Proximate composition and typical protein quality indicators of common African feed ingredients
Ingredient Crude protein (%) Crude fat (%) Crude fibre (%) Key limitation
Soybean meal (full-fat) 35â40 18â20 5â7 Trypsin inhibitors; heat treatment needed
Groundnut cake 40â45 6â8 10â15 Aflatoxin risk; methionine deficiency
Fishmeal (local) 55â65 6â10 1â2 Variable quality; high cost
Cottonseed meal 30â38 2â5 15â20 Gossypol toxicity; lysine deficiency
Brewers' spent grain 18â25 4â7 15â22 High fibre; low digestibility

Sources: FAO (2018), Aquaculture Feed and Fertilizer Resources Information System (AFFRIS); NRC (2011), Nutrient Requirements of Fish and Shrimp; Tacon (1993), Feed Ingredients for Warmwater Fish, FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 306.

Lesson 6: Designing and Conducting Feeding Trials

A well-designed trial gives you data you can trust. Key elements:

  • Objective: Define one clear question â e.g., "Does replacing 30% fishmeal with soybean meal maintain FCR below 1.6?"
  • Treatments and replication: Use at least three replicate tanks or hapas per treatment. Randomise treatment assignment to avoid position bias.
  • Fish: Use uniform size, same age, healthy stock. Acclimatise for 7â14 days before the trial.
  • Feeding: Feed to apparent satiation or at a fixed ration, at the same times daily. Record actual feed offered and adjust for mortalities.
  • Monitoring: Measure water temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH and ammonia daily. Poor water quality confounds feed results.
  • Sampling: Weigh fish at start, mid-point and end. Measure length for condition factor. Record mortalities daily.
  • Duration: 8â12 weeks for growth trials; longer for market-size evaluation.
  • Analysis: Calculate SGR, FCR, PER, survival and feed cost per kg fish. Use simple statistics (ANOVA) to test significance.

In African contexts, trials are often run in earthen ponds, concrete tanks, hapas or cages. Hapas in a pond are cost-effective and allow replication within one water body, but beware of nutrient exchange between hapas and the pond. Tanks give more control but require a reliable water and aeration system.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Feed Handling

Aflatoxin contamination in groundnut cake, maize and cottonseed meal is a serious health risk for fish, farm workers and consumers. Never use mouldy, discoloured or damp ingredients. Store feed in dry, ventilated conditions below 12% moisture. Wear a dust mask when mixing or milling feed to avoid inhaling mould spores and fine particles. If aflatoxin is suspected, do not feed it to fish â the toxin can accumulate in fish tissue and pose a food safety risk. Test suspect batches with an aflatoxin test kit before use. In humid African climates, buy ingredients in quantities you can use within 4â6 weeks.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Sample every incoming ingredient and request proximate analysis before bulk purchase.
  2. Screen new ingredients with in vitro digestibility before committing to in vivo trials.
  3. Use an inert marker (CrâOâ or AIA) for in vivo digestibility and collect faeces consistently.
  4. Calculate FCR, SGR and PER for every trial â not just weight gain.
  5. Run at least three replicates per treatment and randomise tank or hapa assignment.
  6. Monitor water quality daily; poor water quality invalidates feed performance data.
  7. Record all feed offered, mortalities and environmental conditions in a trial logbook.
  8. Convert trial results into cost per kilogramme of fish gained before scaling up.

Further Reading

  • FAO Aquaculture Feed and Fertilizer Resources Information System (AFFRIS) â free database of feed ingredients and nutrient profiles.
  • FAO (2018), Aquaculture Feed and Fertilizer Resources Information System â practical guidance on feed evaluation and formulation.
  • NRC (2011), Nutrient Requirements of Fish and Shrimp â authoritative reference on digestibility and protein quality.
  • FAO (2016), Planning for Aquaculture Diversification â includes feed trial design and species-specific benchmarks.
  • WorldFish Center â free technical reports and training materials on African aquaculture feed and feeding trials.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Use it alongside your farm records to make evidence-based feed decisions that protect margins and improve fish performance.

quiz.q: What does proximate analysis measure?
options: A) Moisture, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre, ash, and NFE
quiz.explanation: Proximate analysis is the standard set of tests for moisture, protein, fat, fibre, ash, and nitrogen-free extract.

quiz.q: Which method is used to determine crude protein in proximate analysis?
quiz.explanation: The Kjeldahl method is the standard for crude protein determination.

quiz.q: What is the ideal crude protein level for catfish fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: Catfish fingerlings require high protein, typically 40-45%.

quiz.q: In proximate analysis, NFE is calculated by:
quiz.explanation: NFE is determined by subtracting moisture, protein, fat, fibre, and ash from 100%.

quiz.q: What is a common marker used in in vivo digestibility trials?
quiz.explanation: Chromic oxide is an inert marker that passes through the fish and is used to calculate digestibility.

quiz.q: In vitro digestibility tests mimic digestion using:
quiz.explanation: In vitro tests use enzymes like pepsin and pancreatin in buffer solutions.

quiz.q: What does a low FCR indicate?
quiz.explanation: A low FCR means less feed is needed per unit of weight gain, indicating better efficiency.

quiz.q: Specific Growth Rate (SGR) is calculated as:
options: A) 100 Ã (ln final weight â ln initial weight) / days
B) Final weight â initial weight
quiz.explanation: SGR is the percentage growth per day, calculated using natural logarithms.

quiz.q: Which of these is a measure of protein quality?
quiz.explanation: Protein Efficiency Ratio (PER) measures weight gain per unit of protein intake.

quiz.q: In a feeding trial, why is replication important?
quiz.explanation: Replicates help account for natural variation and increase the reliability of results.

quiz.q: What is the first step in designing a feeding trial?
quiz.explanation: A clear objective guides all other decisions in the trial.

quiz.q: Which enzyme is used in the stomach phase of in vitro digestibility?
quiz.explanation: Pepsin mimics the acidic stomach environment for protein digestion.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a proximate analysis in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Proximate analysis at African labs usually costs between $20 and $50 per sample.

quiz.q: In vivo digestibility trials require:
options: B) Live fish and faecal collection
quiz.explanation: In vivo trials involve feeding live fish and collecting their faeces.

quiz.q: What does ADC stand for in digestibility trials?
quiz.explanation: ADC is the percentage of a nutrient that is digested and absorbed.

quiz.q: Which fish species typically has a good FCR of 1.0-1.5?
quiz.explanation: Catfish are known for efficient feed conversion, often achieving FCR of 1.0-1.5.

quiz.q: What is the formula for PER?
quiz.explanation: PER is weight gain divided by protein intake.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural marker for digestibility?
quiz.explanation: Acid-insoluble ash can be used as an internal marker without adding chemicals.

quiz.q: What is the recommended number of replicates per treatment in a feeding trial?
quiz.explanation: At least three replicates are recommended for statistical validity.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT measured in proximate analysis?
quiz.explanation: Amino acid profile requires more advanced analysis, not part of proximate analysis.

quiz.q: In a feeding trial, water quality parameters to monitor include:
options: A) Temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, ammonia
quiz.explanation: All these parameters affect fish growth and feed efficiency.

quiz.q: What does a high ash content in maize bran indicate?
options: B) Possible sand or soil contamination
quiz.explanation: High ash suggests inorganic matter like sand.

quiz.q: Which method is used to measure crude fat?
quiz.explanation: Soxhlet extraction with petroleum ether is standard for crude fat.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a marker in digestibility trials?
quiz.explanation: Markers are inert and allow calculation of digestibility by comparing feed and faeces.

quiz.q: In a PER trial, diets must be:
quiz.explanation: To compare protein quality, diets should have the same protein and energy levels.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biological method for protein quality?
quiz.explanation: Net Protein Utilization (NPU) is a biological measure using live animals.

quiz.q: What is the typical duration of a growth trial for tilapia?
quiz.explanation: Most growth trials last 4-8 weeks to see significant differences.

quiz.q: Why is it important to acclimatize fish before a trial?
quiz.explanation: Acclimatization reduces stress and ensures fish are adapted to trial conditions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good FCR for tilapia?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia typically have FCR between 1.2 and 1.8 with good feeds.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of in vitro digestibility over in vivo?
quiz.explanation: In vitro methods are quicker and less expensive than feeding trials.
